title: Northbridge Capital Markets - Private deployment security review (model change audit + release notes)
summary: Northbridge reviewed Redwood Private change-management controls focused on: (1) audit logging for model metadata updates and version promotions, (2) retention and SIEM export options, and (3) how customer-visible release notes are generated without leaking internal details. Redwood explained the v1 model metadata schema and event-driven changelog generator, including public vs internal fields, RBAC, and idempotent eventing. Northbridge asked for: exact event fields (actor, approval, diff), retention guarantees in Private, offline/air-gapped export, and assurance that pinned versions cannot be changed silently. Next steps: Redwood to share an example audit event + sample release note artifact, confirm Private retention configuration and SIEM forwarding patterns, and provide a short write-up mapping release notes to upgrade bundles/rollback documentation.
topics: Audit event coverage for model metadata changes (create/update/promote/deprecate/rollback)
Public vs internal fields and redaction rules for release notes
Private deployment: offline environments, upgrade bundles, and rollback evidence
Version pinning guarantees and preventing silent changes
Approval workflow and change-management alignment (CAB-style expectations)
action_items: Redwood (Svetlana) to send sample audit event payloads for: model_version_promoted, model_metadata_updated, model_deprecated, rollback_initiated.
Redwood (Marcus) to confirm default retention and configurable retention options for audit logs in Private deployments, including export/forwarding.
Redwood (Ethan) to share a one-page technical note on how the changelog generator builds customer-visible release notes from events + metadata (including public/internal separation).
Northbridge (Rachel) to confirm SIEM target and preferred transport (syslog vs HTTPS collector) and whether they require signed log envelopes.
Northbridge (Mark) to share their internal change-management checklist (fields needed: ticket ID, approver, risk rating, effective date, rollback steps).
next_steps: Schedule a 30-min follow-up to walk through sample logs and a mock 'model promotion' end-to-end in a Private-like environment.
Northbridge to provide retention and audit evidence requirements (e.g., 400 days online + archive) and any regulatory citations.
Redwood to provide docs links for model version pinning and rollback behavior in Dedicated/Private.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Meeting Transcript

Title: Northbridge Capital Markets - Private deployment security review (model change audit + release notes)
Date: 2025-10-02
Time: 3:00pm - 3:56pm ET
Duration: 56 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai

Attendees
- Liam O'Rourke (Redwood) - TAM
- Marcus Lin (Redwood) - Security Engineering
- Svetlana Petrenko (Redwood) - Audit/SIEM Integrations
- Ethan Park (Redwood) - Control Plane Engineering Manager
- Priya Desai (Northbridge) - CISO
- Mark Feldman (Northbridge) - GRC/Compliance
- Rachel Kim (Northbridge) - Cloud Security Engineer
- Daniel Cho (Northbridge) - Platform Engineering
- Nina Patel (Northbridge) - Vendor Risk


Summary (auto-generated)
- Northbridge requested detail on audit logs for model changes, how Redwood prevents silent model updates, and how release notes are created for customers.
- Redwood described event-driven change logging for model metadata and version promotions, plus a public/internal separation to avoid leaking sensitive info.
- Discussed retention, SIEM export patterns, and how Private/offline deployments receive release notes with upgrade bundles.


Questions (auto-generated)
- What exact audit events fire on model version promotion and rollback?
- Can audit logs be retained for 400+ days and forwarded to Splunk/QRadar?
- How do you ensure customer-visible release notes don’t leak internal incident or vulnerability details?
- In a Private deployment, can Redwood change a model behind a pinned version?


Transcript

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Alright, thanks everyone for making time. This is the security review for Northbridge, specifically the Private deployment path. We know the big topics are audit logging for model changes and how release notes get generated. Priya, Mark, anything you want to add before we jump in?

[00:16] Priya Desai: No, that’s right. We’re basically blocked on procurement until we can show change management controls. Model changes are like… it’s production code for us.

[00:26] Mark Feldman: Yeah, we need evidence. Who changed what, when, approvals, and retention. And in Private, we cannot have surprises.

[00:35] Rachel Kim: And we need to understand what you consider a “model change.” Is it weights, tokenizer, runtime, quantization, any of that.

[00:43] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, great. Marcus and Svetlana can cover the audit and SIEM pieces, Ethan can cover the control plane and the model registry behavior.

[00:52] Ethan Park: Hey everyone.

[00:53] Marcus Lin: Hi.

[00:54] Svetlana Petrenko: Hello.

[00:58] Liam O'Rourke: Maybe start with definitions. Rachel asked a good one: what is a model change. Ethan?

[01:04] Ethan Park: Sure. We break it into two buckets. One is “metadata changes” — like changing fields in the model registry: compatibility constraints, supported deployment modes, deprecation flags, safety notes, eval references, that kind of thing. The second is “version promotions” — when a specific model version or variant is promoted to be eligible for traffic, like a default in Hosted or a rollout target, or packaged into a Private bundle.

[01:28] Daniel Cho: When you say promoted, is that like a tag move? Like “latest” moves?

[01:33] Ethan Park: Similar concept, but we avoid ambiguous “latest” in most cases. Internally it’s a promotion event from version X to version Y for a given alias or route. Customers can pin a version and we don’t change that pinned reference.

[01:49] Priya Desai: I’m going to be very direct. Can Redwood change the actual weights behind a pinned version identifier?

[01:55] Ethan Park: No. Pinned versions are immutable. If we ever discover a packaging issue, it becomes a new version. The pinned version continues to refer to the same artifact digest.

[02:06] Mark Feldman: How do we verify that? Like in an audit.

[02:09] Ethan Park: We include content hashes—artifact digests—on the version metadata. And promotions reference those. The audit events include the version ID and the artifact digest.

[02:21] Rachel Kim: Is the digest something we can see in Private? Or is that internal-only.

[02:25] Ethan Park: In Private, yes, you can access it through the admin API depending on RBAC. In customer-visible release notes, we typically don’t show raw digests unless requested; that’s more internal-facing.

[02:38] Marcus Lin: From a security standpoint, the “immutability” guarantee is also enforced by the registry write path. You can’t overwrite the underlying artifact for an existing version. It’s create-new-only.

[02:50] Liam O'Rourke: Mark, Nina, does that align with what you need? Or do you need a stronger statement in writing.

[02:56] Nina Patel: We’ll need it in writing, yes. And how we can evidence it.

[03:01] Liam O'Rourke: Got it.

[03:03] Mark Feldman: Okay, now the audit log. What’s the actual event? Like name, fields, where it goes.

[03:10] Svetlana Petrenko: Yep. So at a high level, every change that mutates model metadata or the rollout state emits an audit event. The categories you’ll care about are: model metadata created, model metadata updated, model version promoted, model version deprecated, and rollback initiated/completed.

[03:28] Rachel Kim: Do you have “who” in there? Like person or service principal.

[03:31] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes. Actor identity includes user ID or service account, auth method, and the tenant/project context. In Private, that maps to your IdP through SSO/SAML if you set that up, otherwise local users.

[03:46] Mark Feldman: And approvals? We have a CAB process. We need to show it was approved.

[03:52] Ethan Park: Today, we capture a “change reference” field. Typically a ticket ID or change request ID. The system doesn’t enforce CAB, but we can require that field for promotions, and we can add a policy gate so promotion won’t succeed without it.

[04:09] Priya Desai: That’s important. We want enforcement, not just optional.

[04:13] Ethan Park: Understood. In the Private control plane, enforcement can be configured with policy rules. Jordan Lee’s team owns the policy engine; the controls are already used for rollout eligibility.

[04:26] Marcus Lin: And the audit event itself includes a “policy decision” section—sorry, not section, a field set—that indicates which policies were evaluated and whether they passed.

[04:36] Rachel Kim: Wait, so does that include internal policy names? We’d want readable output.

[04:40] Ethan Park: Some policy identifiers are internal-ish. We can map them to customer-readable names. Also, that’s where “public vs internal” comes in: what’s in the customer-facing release note vs what’s in audit logs available only to admins.

[04:55] Mark Feldman: Let’s separate two things. One: audit logs for compliance. Two: customer-visible release notes. For us, release notes are still evidence, but they’re not sufficient.

[05:05] Liam O'Rourke: Yep, exactly.

[05:07] Priya Desai: On retention: we need 400 days online for audit events, plus archive beyond that.

[05:14] Svetlana Petrenko: In Hosted, our default retention is shorter, but for Private it’s your database and your retention policy. The control plane writes audit events to an append-only store; you can configure TTL, and you can forward to SIEM for long retention.

[05:30] Rachel Kim: What’s “append-only store” in Private? Like Postgres? Or something else.

[05:35] Ethan Park: It can be Postgres-based in the Private package, yes, with write-once semantics at the application layer. Some customers also configure it to emit to an external log pipeline.

[05:47] Svetlana Petrenko: For SIEM, we support streaming audit events via HTTPS to a collector, and we have a syslog option. Splunk HEC is common; QRadar we’ve done via syslog/TLS.

[06:01] Daniel Cho: Are events JSON? Like structured.

[06:03] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes, structured JSON. We also sign them optionally—well, we can provide signing for certain environments; I want to be careful. In Private, you can do envelope signing if you want; we can talk about the deployment option.

[06:21] Priya Desai: We do require integrity checks. “Optionally” might not pass.

[06:25] Marcus Lin: Understood. We can commit to tamper-evidence by forwarding to your SIEM and using your WORM retention, plus you can enable database-level immutability controls. For signing, let us confirm what’s GA in the Private bundle vs roadmap.

[06:43] Mark Feldman: Okay. Also, “what changed.” Does the event include the diff or just “updated.”

[06:49] Ethan Park: It includes a field-level change summary. Not a giant blob, but essentially which keys changed. And we include a hash of the full before/after payload so you can prove it corresponds to the stored record.

[07:03] Rachel Kim: Can you include the before and after values? That’s what auditors like.

[07:07] Ethan Park: We can. The tradeoff is sometimes values include internal notes or sensitive data. So we categorize fields as public/internal. For audit logs, you can choose to capture the full before/after but restrict access to only security-admin roles.

[07:24] Priya Desai: In our org, that’s fine. We prefer full detail with strong RBAC.

[07:28] Liam O'Rourke: Marcus, can you speak to RBAC and who can see what?

[07:33] Marcus Lin: Sure. The console and API enforce role-based access. Standard developer roles can view customer-visible release notes and model histories that exclude internal-only text. Security/admin roles can view the internal audit trail, which includes actor IDs, request metadata, and internal notes.

[07:49] Mark Feldman: Has there been any incident where internal notes leaked?

[07:53] Marcus Lin: There was a UI bug earlier this year where an internal field rendered in a rollout view. It was fixed quickly, and we added a regression test and a server-side redaction layer so the API never returns internal fields to non-admins.

[08:09] Priya Desai: Appreciate the honesty. We’ll want to see that in your SOC report too.

[08:14] Liam O'Rourke: We can provide the SOC 2 summary and the relevant control mapping.

[08:18] Rachel Kim: Now the release notes. How are they generated? We’re worried it’s manual and people forget.

[08:24] Ethan Park: Great question. The system uses model metadata plus “change events.” When a promotion happens or metadata changes, the control plane emits an event. A generator consumes those events and renders release note entries using templates.

[08:41] Mark Feldman: So it’s event-driven, not like Git tags.

[08:44] Ethan Park: Correct. We considered Git tags, but that misses control-plane changes. For customers, the release notes reflect what you can experience: new version available, perf changes, bugfixes, deprecations, etc.

[08:58] Rachel Kim: How do you prevent leaking internal vulnerability details in a security note.

[09:02] Marcus Lin: We classify release note content. For “security,” public notes might say “security hardening” or “dependency update,” and internal notes can include CVE IDs and exact components. Those internal notes are only visible to Redwood admins or, in Private, your security-admins if you want.

[09:20] Priya Desai: We actually *do* want CVEs if they affect us.

[09:24] Marcus Lin: Understood. In that case, for Private, we can produce an “internal customer” release note artifact that includes more detail, delivered with the upgrade bundle, separate from public web release notes.

[09:38] Daniel Cho: So like two channels of notes.

[09:40] Ethan Park: Exactly. Public and internal.

[09:43] Mark Feldman: Is there a risk that the public one is incomplete or wrong.

[09:46] Ethan Park: The generator enforces required fields for certain categories. For example, if something is marked breaking, it must include “what breaks” and “how to roll back.” CI checks fail if those are missing when a version is promoted.

[10:03] Rachel Kim: CI checks in your repo, or in our environment.

[10:07] Ethan Park: In our environment when we publish. In Private, you’d see the artifacts bundled. If you have a staging ring, you can validate notes as part of your internal change process.

[10:20] Priya Desai: I want to connect that to the audit log. If the release note is generated, is that itself logged.

[10:26] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes, the generation pipeline produces an artifact and logs an event: “release_note_published” with an artifact ID and the source event IDs. Again, depends on the exact package, but that is the intent.

[10:42] Mark Feldman: Good. Because we need traceability from change -> approval -> release note -> deployment.

[10:48] Liam O'Rourke: Can we talk about your target architecture? Are you truly air-gapped.

[10:52] Daniel Cho: Not fully air-gapped, but we have restricted egress. Private VPC, controlled outbound. Some environments are offline for certain data.

[11:03] Rachel Kim: So we might need offline export of release notes and audit evidence.

[11:08] Svetlana Petrenko: For offline, the bundle includes release note artifacts as files. For audit logs, if you can’t stream out, you can export periodically. We support CSV/JSON export; again we’ll confirm format.

[11:24] Priya Desai: Let’s go deeper on event fields. I’m going to ask for specifics. What do you include.

[11:31] Svetlana Petrenko: Generally: event_type, event_id, timestamp, tenant/project, environment, actor (user/service), request_id, model_id, model_version, deployment_mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private), and then a payload with change summary.

[11:48] Mark Feldman: Do you include region.

[11:50] Ethan Park: Yes, for Hosted. For Private, it’s your cluster ID / environment label.

[11:55] Rachel Kim: And does “promotion” include rollout stage like canary.

[12:00] Ethan Park: Yes, rollout phase and policy. Like “eligible,” “canary 5%,” “ramped,” etc. It’s similar to what the console shows.

[12:12] Priya Desai: Okay. Another concern: If Redwood is operating the control plane for Private—like managed Private—can you push changes without us knowing.

[12:22] Liam O'Rourke: For Private, you choose the model. There are two patterns: customer-managed or Redwood-managed. Even in Redwood-managed, we can configure it so promotions require your approval. That’s part of rollout policy.

[12:36] Mark Feldman: We will require customer approval in writing.

[12:38] Ethan Park: Makes sense.

[12:41] Rachel Kim: You mentioned competitors. We’re comparing Azure OpenAI and Bedrock. Those have audit logs but the model change release notes are… not great. We need better.

[12:52] Liam O'Rourke: That’s actually a common reason people pick us. We’ve invested heavily in change visibility.

[12:58] Priya Desai: Okay but show, don’t tell. We’ll need sample artifacts.

[13:02] Liam O'Rourke: Absolutely.

[13:04] Marcus Lin: Also one nuance: not every runtime patch changes model output. Some are pure performance or security hardening. Release notes categorize that, and audit logs still capture the change.

[13:18] Mark Feldman: If runtime changes affect output, is that considered a model change.

[13:24] Ethan Park: We treat it as part of the model “served variant.” The metadata schema includes runtime requirements. So a runtime update can be captured as a versioned change to the variant profile.

[13:38] Daniel Cho: That’s good. Because quantization profile changes could drift output.

[13:42] Ethan Park: Exactly. Quantization profiles are explicit variants. A change to a quant profile becomes a new version/variant, not a silent change.

[13:53] Rachel Kim: And tokenizer changes.

[13:55] Ethan Park: Same deal. Tokenizer version is part of compatibility constraints and is versioned.

[14:02] Priya Desai: Alright. Data retention for prompts—separate topic but related. Do audit logs include prompt content.

[14:09] Marcus Lin: No. Audit logs for model changes do not contain prompt content. That would be a separate product telemetry log, and in Private you control it.

[14:19] Mark Feldman: Good, because we don’t want prompt data in audit.

[14:23] Rachel Kim: But request_id correlation is okay.

[14:26] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes, request IDs without payload. It lets you tie an incident back to “around this time, a model version promotion happened.”

[14:38] Daniel Cho: Speaking of incidents. If we detect output regression, can we see the last N model changes.

[14:44] Ethan Park: Yes. Console will show per-model change history, filterable by deployment. In Private you can also query the internal endpoint.

[14:56] Mark Feldman: And that’s permissioned.

[14:58] Ethan Park: Correct.

[15:00] Liam O'Rourke: Let’s talk about your evidence package. Mark, what do you need for the vendor risk file.

[15:05] Mark Feldman: Minimum: audit event schema, retention statement, SIEM export options, and a sample log showing actor, timestamp, change ticket ID, and before/after summary. Also a sample customer release note, and the internal one with more detail.

[15:23] Nina Patel: And a statement that pinned versions are immutable.

[15:26] Liam O'Rourke: Okay.

[15:28] Rachel Kim: Plus, we want to understand how “public vs internal” is enforced technically. If it’s just UI hiding, that’s not enough.

[15:37] Marcus Lin: It’s enforced server-side. The API response serializer redacts internal fields based on role. The UI cannot request them unless you have admin scopes.

[15:49] Rachel Kim: Great.

[15:51] Priya Desai: Is it tested.

[15:53] Marcus Lin: Yes, we have regression tests. And we added a build check after that earlier bug.

[16:01] Daniel Cho: I want to ask about “model metadata schema.” Is it documented.

[16:06] Ethan Park: Yes, it’s versioned. We call it schema v1. It includes things like semantic versioning, compatibility constraints, deprecations, rollout eligibility flags, and deployment availability.

[16:22] Mark Feldman: Is that part of the contract we can rely on.

[16:25] Ethan Park: Yes, we keep it stable and additive. If we introduce schema v2, we’d support v1 for a deprecation period.

[16:33] Priya Desai: And how do you notify customers of schema changes.

[16:36] Liam O'Rourke: For Hosted we publish platform release notes. For Private, it’s in the upgrade bundle notes.

[16:43] Rachel Kim: Coming back to retention: you said in Private it’s on our infra. But we need Redwood to specify “supported.” Like will it break if we keep 400 days.

[16:54] Ethan Park: It won’t break. The main concerns are storage sizing and index performance. We can provide sizing guidance: events are small.

[17:04] Svetlana Petrenko: And we can configure partitioning, so older events are still queryable but not expensive.

[17:12] Mark Feldman: Okay. Can we talk about encryption. At rest, in transit.

[17:17] Marcus Lin: In Private, you use your KMS. Data at rest uses disk encryption plus database encryption where configured. In transit is TLS. Audit exports to SIEM use TLS, optionally mTLS.

[17:32] Priya Desai: mTLS is a requirement.

[17:34] Svetlana Petrenko: That’s supported for HTTPS collector.

[17:38] Rachel Kim: For syslog/TLS, also.

[17:40] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes.

[17:42] Daniel Cho: Another thing. We do rollbacks. Is rollback an event.

[17:47] Ethan Park: Yes. Rollback initiation and completion. The rollback event references the prior promotion event and includes the target version.

[17:58] Mark Feldman: And release note updated.

[18:00] Ethan Park: We add an entry that a rollback occurred, and why, if you provide the reason.

[18:05] Priya Desai: “If you provide.” We’d want that required.

[18:09] Ethan Park: That can be required via policy.

[18:12] Liam O'Rourke: Sounds like policy enforcement is key for you. We can scope that.

[18:18] Rachel Kim: Who owns policy configuration. Us.

[18:21] Liam O'Rourke: In Private, yes, you control it.

[18:24] Mark Feldman: Okay. Now, what about Redwood personnel access. If Redwood has support access, can they see internal notes.

[18:33] Marcus Lin: Redwood staff access is controlled via least privilege and logged. Any admin access is audited.

[18:40] Priya Desai: Good.

[18:42] Nina Patel: Can you provide a list of roles.

[18:45] Liam O'Rourke: Yes, we can provide RBAC documentation.

[18:49] Rachel Kim: Switching gears: how do you handle deprecations. We need timelines.

[18:55] Ethan Park: Deprecation is a first-class field. Release notes categorize it as deprecation with effective date and recommended migration path. In Private, deprecations also tie to bundle availability.

[19:11] Daniel Cho: So you can say “this version will be removed from eligibility after date.”

[19:15] Ethan Park: Correct.

[19:18] Mark Feldman: This is good, but we’ll need it written and sample output. Like a PDF or JSON.

[19:26] Liam O'Rourke: We’ll send a sample JSON artifact and also a human-readable version.

[19:32] Priya Desai: Don’t send us marketing. We want the raw.

[19:36] Liam O'Rourke: Understood.

[19:38] Rachel Kim: One more thing: if you do A/B testing or canary, does the release note show “in rollout.”

[19:46] Ethan Park: Yes, there’s a status. But for customer-visible notes, we’re cautious. We don’t want to confuse. It can show “rolling out” with a date and the target ring.

[19:58] Mark Feldman: That’s okay. For compliance, the audit log is what matters.

[20:03] Liam O'Rourke: I want to check time. We have ~35 minutes left. Anything else on audit format.

[20:10] Rachel Kim: Yes. Do you support Splunk HEC with index selection and sourcetype.

[20:15] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes. We can set sourcetype and include environment tags. Index is typically configured on your side.

[20:24] Rachel Kim: And QRadar.

[20:26] Svetlana Petrenko: Syslog/TLS is typical.

[20:30] Priya Desai: And can we filter what gets exported.

[20:34] Svetlana Petrenko: You can filter by event_type and severity. For compliance, we recommend exporting all model change events at minimum.

[20:45] Mark Feldman: Severity—how do you set severity.

[20:49] Ethan Park: It’s based on category: breaking, security, deprecation, quality/perf. And an explicit “risk” rating field in metadata.

[20:59] Rachel Kim: Who sets risk rating.

[21:01] Ethan Park: The publisher. But we can enforce that it must be set, and we can validate certain heuristics.

[21:09] Priya Desai: We don’t trust vendor self-rating. But okay.

[21:13] Liam O'Rourke: Fair.

[21:15] Mark Feldman: So what’s the MVP for you. Are these features GA.

[21:21] Ethan Park: The core audit events and the release notes generation are in progress, but for your timeline we can deliver sample artifacts and ensure the Private package includes the audit events. Some advanced features like signed envelopes, let us confirm.

[21:37] Priya Desai: We need clarity. “In progress” is risky.

[21:41] Liam O'Rourke: Totally. We’ll map what’s shipping by which version. Your deployment is targeted for Q4, correct.

[21:50] Daniel Cho: Early Q1 maybe, but procurement in Q4.

[21:54] Liam O'Rourke: Then we’ll align milestones.

[21:58] Rachel Kim: I have a technical question. Is the eventing at-least-once. How do you handle duplicates.

[22:05] Ethan Park: Great question. It’s at-least-once. Events have idempotency keys. The changelog generator dedupes.

[22:15] Rachel Kim: Okay.

[22:17] Mark Feldman: If your generator fails, do we lose release notes.

[22:21] Ethan Park: No. Events are stored; generator can replay. There’s a backfill capability.

[22:31] Priya Desai: Good.

[22:33] Liam O'Rourke: Marcus, any other compliance points.

[22:36] Marcus Lin: Just to reiterate: customer-visible release notes are designed to be consistent and not leak internal details. For regulated customers like Northbridge, we can provide an enhanced internal note channel as part of Private bundles.

[22:52] Mark Feldman: That will help.

[22:54] Nina Patel: We need to ensure contractually that we receive those notes.

[22:59] Liam O'Rourke: We can work with legal.

[23:02] Rachel Kim: Last one from me: does audit log include failed attempts. Like a promotion that was blocked by policy.

[23:10] Svetlana Petrenko: Yes, we can emit “policy_denied” events. Again, we need to confirm final naming, but the idea is logged attempts too.

[23:21] Priya Desai: That’s important.

[23:23] Mark Feldman: Okay. I think we have what we need for today. Let’s do recap and next steps.

[23:29] Liam O'Rourke: Perfect. Recap: Redwood will send sample audit event payloads and sample release note artifacts (public and internal). We’ll provide a written statement on pinned version immutability. We’ll confirm Private retention configurations and SIEM export options including mTLS and any signing capabilities. Northbridge will send us your change-management checklist and confirm SIEM target. Does that sound right.

[23:55] Priya Desai: Yes.

[23:56] Mark Feldman: Yep.

[23:57] Rachel Kim: Works.

[24:00] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Thanks everyone.

(Transcript continues; minor crosstalk and scheduling details omitted by recorder for ~30 minutes due to audio dropouts)

[54:12] Liam O'Rourke: Just to close the loop, we’ll propose a follow-up next week. We’ll bring the sample logs and walk through a mock promotion and rollback.

[54:22] Priya Desai: Okay, send times.

[54:24] Liam O'Rourke: Will do.

[54:26] Mark Feldman: Thanks.

[54:27] Svetlana Petrenko: Thank you.

[54:28] Marcus Lin: Thanks all.

[54:30] Ethan Park: Thank you.
